Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 107, verse 1:

(p-114) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Ma'un

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense?﴾ ﴿For that is the one who repulses the orphan,﴾ ﴿and does not urge the feeding of the needy.﴾

"Alladhi yukadhdhibu bi-l-din" (the one who denies the Recompense): the relative pronoun (ism al-mawsul) here is ambiguous (mubham), and what follows it clarifies it, namely "the one who repulses the orphan and does not urge the feeding of the needy."

Allah, Exalted, has clarified in another verse that faith in the Day of Recompense (yawm al-din) impels its possessor to feed the orphan and the needy, in His saying: ﴿And they give food, despite their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾ [al-Insan: 8].

Then He said, explaining the motive behind their feeding them: ﴿We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We do not want from you reward or thanks.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day austere and distressing﴾ [al-Insan: 9-10].

Here there is a question: why did He single out those who deny the Day of Recompense, rather than those who commit these two acts, repulsing the orphan (da', meaning pushing him away and rebuffing him), and not urging the feeding of the needy, and consequently not feeding him from their own means?

The answer: these two are examples and illustrations only.

The first of them is an example of a vile act.

The second is an example of a blameworthy omission.

And since they are two deeds, if they are not Islamic, they are humanitarian before all else.

In the other verse there is a pointer to the answer: the believer fears from Allah a Day that is austere, and He described the Day of Resurrection as "austere" so that he would not frown in the face of the orphan and the needy, given their weakness.

On another side: if denying the Day of Recompense impels one to every ruinous sin, nevertheless (p-115) such sins may find something that restrains them, such as killing, fornication, and wine-drinking, because the right of others is involved; likewise theft and plunder.

As for harming the orphan and neglecting the needy, there is no one who repels it on their behalf, nothing prevents harming these two, and they have no recompense of the kind that those people expect for doing good to them.

Souls are created such that they give only in exchange for something and refrain only out of fear. Fear is secure from the side of the orphan and the needy, and no reward is hoped for from them. Thus no motive remains for doing good to them, and no deterrent against wronging them, except faith in the Day of Recompense and reckoning, whereby a person is held to account even for an atom's weight of good.

It has been said: "repulsing the orphan" means driving him away from his right, and "not urging the feeding of the needy" means not paying zakat.

But the verse contains what prevents this, for zakat is demanded only of the believer, and the context concerns one who denies the Day of Recompense, so there is no zakat for him.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 107, verse 4:

The words of the Most High: ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ ﴿Who are heedless of their prayer﴾.

Scholars have differed concerning the worshippers upon whom the threat of woe is directed here.

The majority (al-Jumhur) hold that they are those who neglect to perform it (the prayer) and are lax regarding the matter of observing it.

It has been said: (the woe is directed at those who are heedless) of its (prayer's) humility (khushu') and of reflecting upon its meanings.

However, the correct view is the first.

It has been reported from ʿAṭāʾ and from Ibn ʿAbbās that they both said: "Praise be to God, who said 'heedless of their prayer' and did not say 'in their prayer'. Just as heedlessness in prayer has never been free from anyone, even the Prophet ﷺ fell into it when he concluded the prayer after two rakʿahs of the Ẓuhr prayer, as is well known from the hadith of Dhu al-Yadayn, and he said: 'I do not forget, but I am made to forget so that I may establish the sunnah.'" So how would God cause him to forget in order to establish for people the rulings of forgetfulness, while people fall into forgetfulness without intending it?

The Prophet ﷺ also said: «My community is excused for error, forgetfulness, and what they are compelled to do.» (p-116)

The jurists have indeed devoted a chapter to the prostration of forgetfulness (sujud al-sahw) as a corrective to this.

Therefore, there remains the question of who is meant by ﴿those who are heedless of their prayer﴾.

It has been said: it was revealed concerning specific individuals by name.

And it has been said: it refers to everyone who delays the prayer beyond its earliest time, or beyond its entire time, and other such things, or who neglects performing it in the mosques and in congregation.

It has also been said: it refers to the hypocrites.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p-466) In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surah al-Ma'un.

The words of the Most High: ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ and the verse.

The ignorant person may imagine from this verse that God has threatened those who pray with woe, while another verse has indicated that not praying is among the causes of entering Saqar, namely His words: ﴿"What has brought you into Saqar?" They will say, "We were not of those who prayed."﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42-43].

The answer to this is entirely clear: the threat of woe is directed at His words: ﴿those who are heedless of their prayer, those who make show (of their deeds)﴾ and the verse [al-Ma'un: 5-6], and they are the hypocrites in truth. We mention this answer despite the weakness of the objection and the clarity of the answer to it, because the heretics (zanadiqah) who do not pray argue for abandoning prayer using this verse.

We have heard from trustworthy people and others that a man said to a wrongdoer who abandons prayer: "What is the matter with you that you do not pray?" He replied: "Because God has threatened woe upon prayer in His words ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾." He said to him: "Recite what follows it." He said: "I have no need of what follows it; what is in it suffices as a warning against prayer." Of this kind is the saying of the poet:

Leave the mosques for the servants to dwell in, and go to the tavern of the wine-seller who pours for us.

"Your Lord did not say, 'Woe to the drunkards,'
But He said, 'Woe to those who pray.'"

So if God Most High has threatened with woe the one who prays yet is heedless of his prayer and makes show in it, how much more so the one who does not pray at all? For him is utter woe, and upon him is the curse of God until the Day of Resurrection, unless he repents.

In the surah there is a clear explanation regarding these people, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who make show of their prayer﴾ ﴿and withhold [simple] assistance﴾ [al-Ma'un: 6-7].

The one who makes a show of his prayer may be a hypocrite (munafiq), and he may be a non-hypocrite.

Showing off (riya') is more general in one respect, and hypocrisy (nifaq) is more general in another respect. That is, a person may show off in one act while being a believer in the Resurrection and the recompense and in all the pillars of faith, and not show off in another act, but rather be sincere in it with complete sincerity.

The hypocrite's outward appearance always contradicts his inner state in everything, not only in prayer.

However, the text has come stating that showing off in prayer is among the deeds of the hypocrites.

The text has also come stating that withholding simple assistance (al-ma'un) is part of human nature, except for those who pray, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious﴾ ﴿when evil touches him, impatient﴾ ﴿and when good touches him, withholding﴾ ﴿except the observers of prayer﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 19-22].

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us, has already explained the neglect of prayer and its loss (idna'uha) at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then there succeeded them successors who neglected the prayer and followed desires, so they will meet evil﴾ [Maryam: 59-60].

At the end of the discussion, under the heading: "A matter concerning the ruling on those who abandon prayer, either by denial or by laziness," he explained it further at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who are maintaining their prayers﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 34], in removing the appearance of contradiction between this verse and the verse ﴿What has caused you to enter Saqar?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42].

(p-117) And he mentioned the poet's saying:

"Leave the mosques to the worshippers to dwell in them,
..."

as we will mention afterward. Then he alerted, saying: "If the threat is for those who are heedless of it, how about those who abandon it?!" End of quote.

Some exegetes have questioned the reason for the juxtaposition of this verse with the one before it.

They answered: All of these are motives for not believing in the Resurrection and causes of denying the Day of Recompense, so they are together with what precedes them in meaning: ﴿For that is the one who repulses the orphan﴾ ﴿and does not encourage the feeding of the poor﴾, and ﴿those who are heedless of their prayer﴾ ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾.

So He grouped them with the first, stated its severe threat, and described them with an attribute, which is that they withhold simple assistance.

NOTICE

In this surah, and in the verse "And those who are steadfast over their prayers" [al-Mu'minun: 9], which is among the attributes of the believers, there is a great contrast.

One of them: concerning the hypocrites who abandon prayer or neglect it.

The other: concerning the believers who maintain it, meaning that prayer is the measure and the dividing line.

On this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The covenant between us and them is prayer; whoever abandons prayer has disbelieved."

As for the effect of prayer in Islam, both on the individual and on the community, it is too great to be mentioned.

We have found some of its effects, which is showing off in deeds, that is, the duality of personality and withholding of al-ma'un (small kindnesses), meaning that one does not extend the hand of help, even in a small way, to the society in which he lives. Clear texts have also come concerning the function of prayer, in this world and the next.

In this world, there is the saying of the Exalted: "Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing" [al-'Ankabut: 45]. Among immorality, in the first degree, is repelling the orphan and not feeding the needy.

(p-118) Among its effects is that every evil vice is forbidden. It is thus a barrier for the person that guards him from every vice. It is also a help in every hardship, as the Exalted said: "And seek help through patience and prayer" [al-Baqarah: 45], so He made it the companion of patience in overcoming difficulties. In the Hereafter, it is a light, as the Exalted said: "On the Day you will see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and at their right hands" [al-Hadid: 12], together with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "My ummah will come on the Day of Resurrection with bright faces and white limbs from the traces of wudu'."

As for His saying: "and withhold al-ma'un" [al-Ma'un: 7], it was said: al-ma'un here is zakah, because of its small amount. Al-ma'un means little, and al-ma'un also means property in the dialect of Quraysh.

It was also said: it is whatever helps in any work, such as the bucket, the axe, the needle, the cooking pot, and the like.

Since neglect of prayer leads to withholding al-ma'un, one who withholds al-ma'un, which is a tool or vessel by which a need is met and then returned as it was without loss, will certainly withhold charity or zakah, and this is more so.

From here: the hypocrite would not pay his wealth in zakah, nor give charity to the needy, nor even lend another a goodly loan. Therefore we find that usury spreads more widely and more severely among hypocrites.

Here two discussions arise. The first: the ruling on showing off (riya') and its definition. The second: the ruling on lending (ariyah).

As for riya': it was said that it is derived from ru'yah (seeing), and what is meant by it is displaying worship in order that people see it and praise one for it. It has come in a hadith naming it "the hidden shirk": "Indeed, what I fear most for you is hidden shirk." They said: "What is hidden shirk, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Riya', for it is more hidden in your souls than the crawling of an ant."

The saying of the Exalted also came: "So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord" [al-Kahf: 110].

The explanation of shirk in it is that one performs an act which is originally for Allah, such as prayer, charity, or Hajj, but displays it in order that people praise him for it.

(p-119) Thus this part of it is a partnership with Allah, since part of his deed has become sought for the praise of people.

The hadith of Abu Hurayrah is in Muslim: Allah the Exalted says: "I am the most independent of partners from partnership. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his shirk."

As for the ruling on riya' in deeds, in this text there is an indication that the deed is returned to its doer and rejected by Him.

It was said: it is neither for him nor against him.

It was said: it is not free of blame, as Allah warned against it by His saying: "And do not be like those who went out from their homes in insolence and to be seen by people" [al-Anfal: 47].

In the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever shows off, Allah will show him off; and whoever seeks to be heard, Allah will make him heard." Narrated by Muslim.

Tasmi' is doing an act so that people will hear of it, as in the hadith about the wedding feast: "On the first, second, and third day it is sum'ah (showing off). Whoever makes it heard, Allah will make him heard by it."

So riya' refers to seeing, and tasmi' refers to hearing.

It is known that these verses were revealed concerning Quraysh on the day of Badr, and Allah nullified their deeds and turned them back on their heels.

In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and it was said: it nullifies deeds in the sense of the name of shirk, because of His saying: "Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with" [al-Nisa': 48].

It is answered: it nullifies only the deed in which one is engaged. If one shows off in prayer, it nullifies that prayer and does not extend to fasting. If one shows off in a voluntary prayer, its nullification does not extend to an obligatory prayer, and so on. One may begin a deed sincerely for Allah, then the shadow of riya' comes upon it. Is his deed preserved, or does the riya' that arose in it nullify it?

They said: if it was a passing thought and he repelled it, it does not harm him; if he indulged in it, then [it harms him]. Ahmad and Ibn Jarir preferred that the deed is not nullified, considering the soundness of the intention at the beginning.

Their evidence in this: what Abu Dawud related in his Maraseel from 'Ata' al-Khurasani: "A man said: O Messenger of Allah, the whole of Banu Salamah fights; some fight for worldly gain, some fight out of zeal, and some fight seeking the Face of Allah, the Exalted. He said: 'All of them, if the origin of his affair is that the Word of Allah be supreme.'"

It was mentioned from Ibn Jarir that this applies to a deed whose end is linked to its beginning, such as prayer and fasting.

As for what is like recitation and knowledge, it requires renewing the sincere intention for Allah, because each part of recitation and each part of seeking knowledge is independent in itself and not linked to what precedes it.

There is a question: a servant performs a deed purely for Allah, then some people become aware of it and praise him well, and this pleases him. There is no disagreement that this is not riya' at all, because of what came in the hadith of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about a man who does good and people praise him for it. He (ﷺ) said: "It is the immediate glad tidings for the believer." Narrated by Muslim.

Some scholars mentioned that whoever performs a deed in secret, then some people come and he leaves it for their sake, fearing riya', he enters into riya', because he becomes weak in purifying his intention for Allah. In this there is remoteness and hardship.

* *

As for withholding al-ma'un and giving it, which is lending (ariyah) as has preceded.

The discussion of ariyah has two aspects: what ariyah is, and second, its ruling, whether it is obligatory or permissible, and the ruling on its liability, whether it is guaranteed or not.

As for its definition among the jurists: it is permission to benefit from a specific item of property while its substance remains.

Their phrase "while its substance remains" applies to the cooking pot, the axe, the needle, the sieve, and the like, unlike what is consumed in its use, such as candle for light, oil for anointing, kohl for application, and the like, which are used up by use. These are not ariyah but a loan (qard), and the exchange of a loan is by its like.

As for the ruling on ariyah: it was said: it is permissible.

(p-121) It was said: rather, it is obligatory.

It was said: it is recommended.

Ibn Qudamah related consensus on its being recommended. The evidence of those who say it is obligatory is the text of the verse: "and withhold al-ma'un," and the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning camels, when he mentioned zakah: "and its right is lending its bucket, allowing its stallion to serve, and giving its milk on the day of watering."

In reality, this hadith mentions things which are certainly not ariyah, such as stallion service and giving milk, which weakens the use of it as evidence.

Al-Majd cited it in al-Muntaqa with the narration of Ahmad and others.

As for the threat in the verse, they said: it is directed at the three attributes together: neglect of prayer, showing off in deeds, and withholding al-ma'un. Whoever has one of them has his share of the threat according to it.

The least that can be said about it is what came in His saying: "and cooperate in righteousness and piety" [al-Ma'idah: 2], and the authentic hadith concerning zakah, "when the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned gold, silver, camels, cattle, and horses, and said: 'and he does not forget Allah's right in its back.'"

Then "he was asked about donkeys, and he said: 'I have not received anything about them except the lone unique verse: "So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it"' [al-Zalzalah: 7]."

Lending goods is permission of benefit, and it is a great good.

The other hadith: "The property of a Muslim man is not lawful except with his good pleasure."

Al-Shawkani quoted from al-Kashshaf an opinion that it is obligatory in case of necessity, and that refusing it outside necessity is disgraceful and contrary to manliness. End quote.

Necessity is like a bucket when you come to water and have no bucket with you, and in need of water.

The analogy of the jurists is that if something is destroyed because of that, the one who withheld it is liable.

As they said regarding refraining in some cases: is it an act or an omission? Like someone who has thread which is needed to sew a person's wound, or cotton, and the person dies; is withholding the thread merely an omission for which one is not held accountable, or is it considered an act because the death of a person resulted from it? Similarly, withholding a bucket so that one may drink or water his camel, or drink himself?

(p-122) The correct view among them is that omission in such a situation is held accountable as an act, as the author of Maraqi al-Su'ud said:

"And omission is an act according to the sound position."

Here there is what the correct Arabic usage supports, as was said about building the mosque:

"If we sit while the Prophet is working, that would be misguided work from us."

So sitting out of work was called "misguided work." It follows from this that ariyah is recommended by the Shari'ah and by manliness and custom in a state of choice, and obligatory in a state of necessity, with the note that most cases of borrowing are of necessity, though the circumstances of necessity vary.

Allah praised the Ansar, that they "prefer others over themselves, even though they themselves are in need" [al-Hashr: 9]. So lending is even more so, since it is benefited from and returned to its owner.

The poet also praised a people for not withholding al-ma'un, saying:

"A people upon Islam who have not withheld their al-ma'un, and do not neglect the tahlil."

Although some people took al-ma'un here to mean zakah, the poet's saying "a people upon Islam" implies that they pay zakah as part of their Islam, so the remainder is an extension of their condition regarding al-ma'un specifically.

The remaining discussion is its liability. Opinions differ on whether ariyah is guaranteed. Some consider it a trust (amanah), and accordingly it is not guaranteed; this is the position of the Hanafis and Malikis, provided no transgression occurred on the borrower's part.

According to al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, it is guaranteed, unless it was used in the permitted manner.

As they said regarding the sword: if one borrows it and it breaks in battle, there is no liability for it.

Those who hold it guaranteed cite the general hadith: "On the hand is what it has taken until it returns it," narrated by (p-123) al-Majd in al-Muntaqa, who said: narrated by the five except al-Nasa'i.

And the hadith of Safwan ibn Umayyah: "that the Prophet (ﷺ) borrowed from him on the day of Hunayn some armor, said to be thirty, said to be eighty, said to be a hundred. He said: 'Is it by usurpation, O Muhammad?' He said: 'Rather, it is a guaranteed loan.' He said: 'Some of it was lost,' so the Prophet (ﷺ) offered to guarantee it for him. He said: 'Today I am more eager in Islam.'" Narrated by Ahmad and Abu Dawud.

The jurists stated that its liability is by its value on the day it was destroyed, or by its like if it is fungible. This is supported by what came in the case of Hafsah's bowl, when 'A'ishah struck it and it fell to the ground and broke, and the food scattered. The Prophet (ﷺ) took 'A'ishah's bowl and returned it to Hafsah, saying: "A bowl for a bowl, and food for food." That is, liability is by the like if it is fungible, or by value if it is valued.

If ariyah is guaranteed and its ruling is permissibility, the borrower may ask to return it whenever he wishes, unless the borrower's interest is tied to it, and it cannot be returned except with harm to him.

They said: it is like one who lent a ship, and the borrower took it into the middle of the sea. The lender cannot then reclaim it, since that is impossible in the middle of the sea.

It is said: he may demand it back, and the cost falls upon the borrower. The first view is more preponderant.

And like one who lent land for planting, and before the crop is harvested its owner demands it back, and so on. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

The ruling on one who denies a loan (al-'ariyah)

The story of the Makhzumite woman is well known: she used to borrow goods and deny them, and she became famous for this. Then she stole, and her hand was cut off for the theft, not for denying the borrowed goods. This is the more correct view, because theft occurs only in secret and from a protected place (hirz).

Borrowing (al-isti'arah) is the opposite of that, and it falls under the Almighty's saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts to their owners﴾ [al-Nisa': 58].

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The hand is responsible for what it has taken until it returns it."

And the hadith: "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you." Related by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, who said: it is a hasan hadith.

This is a summary of the topics of 'ariyah. Its detailed branches are in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh). From it we have abridged what relates to withholding small household goods (al-ma'un) and the impermissibility of withholding them, and what relates to giving them freely. And success is from Allah the Exalted.

A caution

In this surah there is a demonstration of a scholarly method binding on every researcher: gathering the extremes of the texts and not restricting oneself to one part of them. This is seen in the Almighty's saying: ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ [al-Ma'un: 4]. This is an independent verse, and if taken alone it would be a threat to those who pray.

As the dissolute poet said:

Leave the mosques to the worshippers to dwell in them, and go to the wine-tavern, which pours for us.
Your Lord did not say "woe to those who are drunk," but He said "woe to those who pray."

Therefore it is necessary to join to it what follows, for explanation and clarification: ﴿those who are heedless of their prayer﴾, and then this explanation is itself further explained by His saying: ﴿those who make show [of their deeds]﴾ ﴿and withhold small kindnesses﴾.

Similar to this verse in hadith is what is found in Ibn Majah, with its chain, from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "It was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'The water-channel (maysarah) of the mosque has fallen into disrepair.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever restores the maysarah of the mosque, two portions of reward will be written for him.'"

This hadith, though it is in the Zawa'id, al-Busiri said of it: in its chain is Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, who is weak. Nevertheless, it is explicit regarding what it illustrates, for whoever restricts himself to his answer (ﷺ) will regard the maysarah of the mosque as the more excellent, while whoever joins both ends of the hadith understands its intended meaning.

Based on this is what Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) adopted in the chapter on testimony: that a person may not testify upon a mere statement he heard, unless they ask him to testify to it and say "bear witness to it," or unless he heard the report from its beginning, lest the beginning contain something linked to its end. For example, if a speaker says to another: "I have a horse with you, and you have a hundred dirhams with me," and he hears only his words "you have a hundred dirhams with me" without what came before, then if he testifies to what he heard, it would harm the one testified against. This surah supports this line of reasoning. And Allah the Exalted knows best.
